note.title: Choosing an Algorithm Design Method
steps: Identify the steps and decisions needed to solve the problem.
Use a flowchart when you want to show the overall flow visually.
Use pseudocode when you want to describe the logic step by step in words.
Check that each decision has the correct branches and that the process can reach an end.
note.answer: Flowcharts and pseudocode are two ways to describe an algorithm. Flowcharts use graphical symbols and arrows. Pseudocode uses plain language and a structured format.

written.text: Q7.2. Explain how you would use algorithm design methods, such as flowcharts and pseudocode, to solve a complex computational problem. Illustrate your explanation with a detailed example.
written.finalAnswer: Use a flowchart to show the steps and decision branches, and pseudocode to state the detailed logic; for example, both can describe assigning a grade from a student's marks.

rubric.description: Show how the methods work together to solve the example.
rubric.how: Explain that the flowchart shows the branches and pseudocode gives the detailed steps, ending with the assigned grade.

modelAnswer: First, understand the problem and identify the input, processing steps, decisions, and output.
A flowchart can show the steps using symbols: a parallelogram for input and output, a rectangle for a process, a diamond for a decision, and arrows for flow.
Pseudocode can then describe the same logic in a structured, readable form without using the syntax of a particular programming language.
For example, to assign a grade, the input is a student's marks and the output is the grade.
Check the marks in descending order: if marks are at least 90, assign A+; otherwise if they are at least 80, assign A.
Continue with the same method: at least 70 gives B; at least 60 gives C; otherwise assign F.
The flowchart shows each marks decision as a diamond with branches leading to the grade output.
The pseudocode records these conditions in order, making the logic clear and ready to convert into a program.

written.text: Q7.8. Compare and contrast flowcharts and pseudocode as methods for algorithm design. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each method, and provide examples where one might be preferred over the other.
written.finalAnswer: Flowcharts use graphical symbols and arrows to show an algorithm visually; pseudocode uses plain, structured language to describe it in detail. Flowcharts help show overall flow and decisions, while pseudocode is useful for detailed planning and conversion into code.

rubric.description: Discuss the advantages or limitations of the methods.
rubric.how: Explain that flowcharts make overall flow intuitive to see, while detailed diagrams can be less convenient to change or read when complex.

rubric.why: Examples show how a student would choose between the methods.
rubric.description: Give examples and a final comparison.
rubric.how: Prefer flowcharts for seeing decisions at a glance and pseudocode for detailing logic that will be converted into code.

modelAnswer: Flowcharts and pseudocode both describe algorithms, but they use different forms.
Flowcharts use graphical symbols and arrows to represent the flow of an algorithm.
Their advantage is that the overall process and its decisions can be understood at a glance; they are useful for identifying steps and branches visually.
A flowchart can be preferred when explaining a process such as checking whether an item is available and then choosing a branch.
Pseudocode uses plain language and a structured format to describe algorithm steps sequentially.
It is useful for planning and explaining logic without worrying about programming syntax, and it can be converted into actual code in any programming language.
Pseudocode can be preferred when giving detailed instructions for checking a username and password or testing whether a number is prime.
Thus, flowcharts are more visual, while pseudocode is more detailed and easier to translate into code; the suitable method depends on the problem and purpose.

examTips: Short questions may ask for the definition and use of flowcharts or pseudocode, or ask you to distinguish between them.
For flowchart questions, marks are commonly earned by naming the correct symbols and showing the order and direction of steps with arrows.
For pseudocode questions, write steps in a clear order and include the conditions and both outcomes of a decision.
For comparison questions, describe both methods and give a clear difference or suitable example for each.
In pseudocode, use the section's notation such as if, then, else, End if, for, return, and %.

explain.title: Flowcharts
explain.body: Flowcharts are visual representations of the steps in a process or system, depicted using different symbols connected by arrows. They help people see a process and its decisions clearly.

explain.title: Flowchart symbols
explain.body: An oval represents the start or end. A rectangle represents a process or task. A parallelogram represents input or output. A diamond represents a decision. An arrow, or flowline, shows the direction of flow.

explain.title: Pseudocode
explain.body: Pseudocode is a method of representing an algorithm using simple and informal language that is easy to understand. It is not actual code that can be run on a computer; it helps you focus on the algorithm's logic without worrying about programming syntax.

explain.title: Choosing a method
explain.body: Flowcharts show the flow visually, which helps you see the overall structure and decisions. Pseudocode describes each step in a structured, readable way and is useful when planning how to turn an algorithm into code.

explain.title: Decisions in algorithms
explain.body: A decision checks a condition and chooses a path. In a flowchart, the decision is shown with a diamond and branches such as Yes and No. In pseudocode, the decision can be written with if, then, else, and End if.

mistakes: Using a rectangle for a decision instead of a diamond.
Using a parallelogram for a process instead of for input or output.
Leaving out arrows or making the direction of flow unclear.
Forgetting to show both outcomes of an if/else decision.
Calling pseudocode executable program code; pseudocode is an informal way to describe an algorithm.
In the even-or-odd example, using = instead of == in the condition shown in the textbook.
In the prime-number example, forgetting to return False for numbers less than or equal to 1.
